# Discussion

Numerous studies have shown that climate warming, nitrogen deposition, and increased grazing can all lead to plant diversity losses [@klein2004experimental; @kaarlejarvi2017herbivores; @wu2020additive; @shangguan2024plant; @anderson2025experimental; @Austrheim2001-nu; @klein2004experimental; @niedrist2009plant; @Bernes2015-yg; @post2023large]. We also found the typical negative effects on diversity of nitrogen deposition in this study as well as of warming in the sub-alpine. However, diversity actually increased with warming along most of the nitrogen gradient in the alpine and clipping had only minimal net effects on diversity. In this study, we take a step further by disentangling the direct and indirect effects of these three global change drivers, to understand their underlying mechanisms and to generalize across drivers and climate context. Specifically, we tested whether these global change drivers all operate on diversity indirectly, mediated through community biomass, which reflects the magnitude and type of competition. If that were true, knowing general patterns and trends in community biomass of plants could predict changes in plant diversity rather than needing to understand all the direct effects of different drivers. 

We found only partial support for our hypothesis, with indirect effects through community biomass having substantial effects in the alpine community, but relatively little impact in the sub-alpine community. Warming also had direct effects on diversity in both communities, while direct effects of nitrogen addition were only found in the sub-alpine community. Below, we explore community biomass-mediated effects on diversity in this experiment and the mechanisms underlying the direct effects of each of the global change drivers, including why both direct and indirect mechanisms might differ between the alpine and sub-alpine communities. Finally, we discuss the implications for our ability to generalize impacts of global change drivers.

### Community biomass mediates effects of global change on diversity

There was a negative indirect effect of all three global change drivers mediated through biomass in both communities, although it was only significant in the alpine community (@fig-cut-final-diversity). Nevertheless, species' environmental affinities suggest that community biomass plays an important role even in the sub-alpine community. The net indirect effect of the global change drivers on the diversity indices tended to be negative, except for richness in the sub-alpine community (Supplement Figure S6), suggesting greater local extinction than colonization and/or increasing dominance in most cases. For both communities, we see a significant shift towards more light-demanding species with increasing community biomass, suggesting greater competition for light [e.g. @olsen2016facilitation]. A similar shift is evident in both communities for the warming and nitrogen addition treatments, which has been observed previously [@Klanderud2005-yx; @Wang2012-cj; @Fu2016-dw]. One possible explanation of the lack of significant biomass-mediated effect on diversity at the sub-alpine community is that the alpine community was more temperature and nutrient limited therefore simply had a bigger change in biomass in response to warming and nitrogen addition (XXX, Supplement Figure S5). In turn, this would lead to a smaller impact on diversity. A complementary explanation is that the sub-alpine is more productive in unmanipulated conditions (Supplemental Table 2) and therefore may already have intense competition for light. Even with a similar magnitude of biomass response to warming or nitrogen, many light-demanding species may already be absent (consistent with @fig-toenails), leaving less room for further diversity loss. If these arguments are correct, it suggests that less productive communities are likely to see the biggest declines in diversity from global change.

Clipping and grazing effects on the diversity indices were always mediated through community biomass, except for a direct clipping effect on evenness in the sub-alpine community. In line with many other studies, we found that clipping prevented the loss of diversity and evenness under warming and nitrogen levels above 10 kg N ha^-1^ y^-1^ in the alpine community (@fig-1-biomass-diversity b), suggesting this was related to competitive release [@Austrheim2001-nu; @klein2004experimental; @niedrist2009plant; @Bernes2015-yg; @kaarlejarvi2017herbivores; @post2023large]. Interestingly, higher biomass and warming led to a shift to species with higher grazing tolerance in the alpine, but not in the sub-alpine community. In the same experiment, we have shown that warming shifts the alpine community to more resource acquisitive traits [@halbritter2025effects], suggesting a shift towards a community with a higher tolerance for grazing [@lebbink2024plant; @archibald2019unified].

### Direct effects of global change on diversity

Warming had a direct positive effect on diversity, species richness, and evenness in the alpine community (@fig-cut-final-diversity), which likely reflects a combination of increase in abundance of warm-adapted species and colonization by species with a higher temperature requirement from the vegetation surrounding the transplanted community. This is supported by a strong shift in the distribution of temperature affinities with warming (@fig-toenails b). In contrast, in the sub-alpine community, warming had a strong negative direct effect on diversity and species richness, but without any accompanying shift in distribution of species' temperature affinity, which were already quite high even in unmanipulated conditions. Instead, the loss of species seems to be related to a loss of drought-tolerant species. This was somewhat surprising since we expected and found warming to be generally associated with a decline in soil moisture in both sites (Supplement Figures 1 and 2, Supplement Table 1). The observed opposite direct effects of warming on diversity in the two communities might be explained by confounding effects between termperature and moisture affinities of the species. Warming shifted the alpine community towards warm demanding species which had a similar tolerance in moisture (@fig-toenails b), while the sub-alpine plant community consisted of already highly temperature demanding species (i.e. high temperature affinities with narrow distribution), and warming therefore shifted the community towards species with a higher moisture tolerance (i.e. *Carex bigelowii*, *C. pilulifera*, and *Phleum alpinum* that have medium moisture affinities were lost). Overall, warming can have strong direct effects on plant diversity [@white2014direct].

Nitrogen addition had a direct negative effect on diversity in both communities, but the effect was much stronger and significant in the sub-alpine community, where evenness, but not richness decreased. This suggests a shift in abundance of species rather than a loss of species. This is unlikely due to a shift in nutrient demanding species since such a shift only occurred in the alpine community and was very small in the sub-alpine community. Species' environmental affinities however suggest that the strong direct effect of nitrogen addition was a consequence of acidification following fertilizing [@Kimmel2020-fo]. In both communities, there was a strong and significant shift towards more acid tolerant species with increasing nitrogen. The acidification could have been stronger in the sub-alpine community, because that community is less nutrient limited, generally, although not always associated with an increase in available calcium at high levels of nitrogen addition, which can be released from the bedrock under acid conditions.

Consistent with the minimal net effects of clipping on diversity (@fig-1-biomass-diversity b), clipping and grazing had no direct effects on diversity, except that clipping decreased evenness directly in the sub-alpine community. Similarly, none of the measured species' environmental affinities showed any shifts due to clipping. Species loss was reduced at both clipping intensities, but only the intensive clipping treatment significantly increased diversity, suggesting that the medium clipping treatment was too low to effectively reduce competition for light in this community (i.e. less biomass reduction, @fig-1-biomass-diversity a). ### Interesting stuff about biomass and stronger T and N limitation in the alpine

Our main hypothesis was that the three global change drivers, warming, nitrogen addition, and clipping, operate through increased community biomass favoring more intense competition, especially for light, resulting in a decrease in vascular plant diversity. In line with the first part of this hypothesis, we found a strong increase in community biomass with warming and nitrogen addition in both alpine and sub-alpine communities, paralleling the findings of previous studies manipulating one or both of these drivers [@elmendorf2012plot; @Humbert2016-wg; @Zhang2023-xg]. Warming can increase biomass because of higher rates of photosynthesis, a longer growing season, or because higher microbial activity can increase nutrient availability, while nitrogen addition directly increases nutrient availability. The alpine site was strongly temperature and nutrient limited, resulting in a four to five times increase of community biomass with either warming or nitrogen addition. This co-limitation at the alpine site could be an explanation for the stronger mediation through biomass compared to the sub-alpine site. <!-- Last sentence, needs more explanation -->

### Conclusions and implications

Our findings show that community biomass can be used as a general indicator of mechanisms mediating global change impacts on plant diversity, but this was only true in colder and unproductive alpine grassland. Several of these drivers including warming, nitrogen addition, clipping, and grazing work through the same mechanisms. However, at the same time, we also found that some drivers including warming and nitrogen addition operate through multiple mechanisms. This means that only including community biomass only works partially, and might miss some of the direct effects. <!--So, we find that our framework does not really work. It only works in the alpine, and there are still strong direct effect. What is our suggestion then? You still need to include both direct and indirect effects?You get quite a lot of variation explained by effects on biomass in both cases, right? But the influence of other mechanisms (direct effects) appear to be more important in warmer environments. This is really interesting I think, and warrents further investigation of what these mechanisms could be, and whether you see this in other places (new expts) -->

The relative importance of the drivers was not consistent across sites, advocates for replicating experiments across gradients and landscapes to allow more general understanding of ecological processes [@fraser2013coordinated; @prager2022integrating]. Our results showed that community proxies, such as environmental affinities can help to get a more general understanding of the underlying ecological processes.

\[*is this useful?*\] Our study was conducted over three years and thus looks at short-term responses, which can differ from long-term responses[(*56*, *57*)](https://paperpile.com/c/KKq9O1/egX7+3xXg). Long-term experiments across different climatic contexts are needed to understand where and how local adaptation of grazing regimes can be used as a tool to mitigate impacts of warming and pollution and inform adaptive management strategies that benefit biodiversity. <!--probably a caveat you need to mention-->

<!--Higher up-->

The major change in community biomass, diversity and evenness occurred at levels of nitrogen addition beyond 10 kg N ha\^-1\^ y^-1^, which is the critical load for significant changes in the structure and function of alpine and sub-alpine grasslands (35). This similar relationship between the warmed alpine and ambient sub-alpine communities suggests that colder alpine plant communities are not intrinsically less productive than those at lower elevation, but are limited by temperature-related environmental factors (27).

<!--Higher up-->

Since the overall grazing effects were similar compared to clipping, it suggests that our simulated grazing treatment is comparable to natural grazing and that additional effects of grazing, such as different timing of biomass removal, trampling, and fertilization from the animals did not override the effect of biomass removal per se.

<!-- Interesting, but I don't see that this fits here -->

Interestingly, diversity indices based on change in abundance (i.e. evenness and diversity) showed more change in the cold alpine community in response to global change drivers, while indices based on change in species turnover (i.e. species richness and diversity), changed more in the warmer sub-alpine community. This might be because community changes in cold environments (i.e. the alpine) are often slow[(*45*)](https://paperpile.com/c/KKq9O1/ot2B) and changes in biomass (i.e. abundance) generally happen faster than species turnover (i.e. colonization or extinction) and there is often an extinction lag in alpine communities[(*14*, *15*, *46*)](https://paperpile.com/c/KKq9O1/ztDH+wbqE+5luD).
